text: In the Hanbury Brown-Twiss setup, why is the light split onto TWO detectors rather than measured with one?
choices: To double the total photon count rate
Because a single detector cannot register single photons at all
To measure first-order coherence g1 instead of g2
To defeat single-detector dead time and afterpulsing, making the tau-to-zero correlation accessible
explanation: Splitting onto two detectors lets a coincidence at zero delay be recorded despite each detector's dead time and afterpulsing, so g2(tau-to-0) becomes measurable and the cross-correlation equals the input auto-correlation. HBT measures g2, not g1 (choice 2); the goal is correlation access, not raw count rate (choice 0); single detectors do register photons (choice 1).
